Abstract Digital repositories play a crucial role in promoting green computing initiatives by supporting paperless practices and sustainable resource use. It offers a sound infrastructure to store, manage, and reuse digital materials. With the advancement of the Internet of Things (IoT), smart data-capturing technologies have been integrated into digital repositories, a development that has gained even greater relevance since the COVID-19 pandemic, which increased demand for digital documentation in higher education due to online classes, meetings, and auditing processes. Despite these advantages, adoption remains limited in higher education institutions because of low awareness and usability concerns. This study examines the determinants of digital repository adoption among staff and students in the Malaysia Technical University Network (MTUN) using the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), with green attitude integrated into the framework. A quantitative approach using a stratified sampling method has yielded 199 valid responses. The data was analysed using Partial Least Squares-Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). The findings reveal that performance expectancy, facilitating conditions (technological constructs), and green attitude (a psychosocial construct) significantly influenced staff intentions to use digital repositories, while only green attitude influenced students. These results highlight the importance of cultivating a green mindset in encouraging adoption and demonstrate the role of digital repositories in advancing sustainability. The study contributes to the literature on technology adoption in higher education and aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals No. 4: “Quality Education,” No. 12: “Responsible Consumption and Production,” and No. 13: “Climate Action,” offering actionable insights for university policymakers to strengthen green digital infrastructure. Keywords: psychosocial, green digital infrastructure, UTAUT, technology acceptance, technology adoption 1. Introduction The rapid growth of globalization and advancements in digital technology have made higher education a crucial catalyst for economic growth, innovation, and human capital development (Volchik et al., 2018; Maneejuk & Yamaka, 2021). Owing to the global transformation, countries around the world must adapt to global pressures toward technological advancements. This situation has reinforced the growing importance of higher education in producing skilled graduates who can contribute to the country's economic growth. Notably, several past studies have emphasised a significant positive relationship between education and national economic performance (Goczek et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024). The evolution of the digital economy and Industrial Revolution 4.0 (IR 4.0), as well as the COVID-19 epidemic, has significantly accelerated the revolution of the higher education landscape (Sharma, 2019; Lehmann et al., 2023; Mayer et al., 2023). Within this framework, digital repositories are essential, as they can provide institutions with a centralised platform for managing, storing and accessing educational resources. In Malaysia, initiatives such as the Smart School Programme (Chris et al., 2006), the Malaysian Research and Education Network (MyREN) (Rohani & Ow, 2012), the National e-Learning Policy (DePAN 2.0) (Kementerian Pendidikan Tinggi Malaysia, 2015), and massive open online courses (MOOCs) (Fadzil et al., 2016; Azrina, 2015) demonstrate national efforts towards enhancing the digital education infrastructure. Moreover, the COVID-19 pandemic further stressed the need for adaptable and flexible digital learning environments (Ali & Georgiou, 2024; Lehmann et al., 2023; Maican et al., 2025). Programmes such as Malaysia's 2H2U (2 years at home, 2 years at university), which is also known as flexible learning, illustrate the transition towards a hybrid learning environment and stress the importance of digital repositories in maintaining continuity and accessibility in higher education (Mohamed, 2023; Raghunathan et al., 2022). Digital repositories offer an environmentally friendly option, reducing resource consumption and supporting climate action goals. In contrast, conventional paper-based processes, which are common in education, significantly contribute to environmental degradation through high CO emissions driven by the high demand for paper and increased energy 2 consumption from printing activities (Ali et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2019). Like other types of technology, the adoption of digital repositories is also shaped by various behavioural factors. Typically, users are interested in using any technology when the technology features are user friendly, supportive, and capable of simplifying or enhancing their tasks (Ayanwale & Ndlovu, 2024; Menon & Shilpa, 2023). The literature consistently emphasises the relevance of the UTAUT constructs (performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions) in explaining user adoption of technology (Fagan, 2019; Kelly et al., 2023). Nevertheless, findings have varied across contexts (Lin, 2019; Mensah, 2019), indicating that users’ behaviour is likely influenced by situational and institutional factors. As such, despite the potential benefits, some institutions' adoption rates of digital repositories remain low (Ezema & Eze, 2024). This condition might be due to inadequate awareness and a lack of knowledge of their potential advantages (Vimal et al., 2023), insufficient infrastructure, and technical support (Ezema & Eze, 2024). Predominantly, most studies have focused on investigating users’ intention to adopt digital libraries and information systems (Abeysekera et al., 2024), whereas research examining the adoption of digital repositories in higher education remains relatively limited (Anistyasari et al., 2018). Surprisingly, a substantial gap was found in the literature concerning the technological and psychosocial factors that influence such adoption. To address this, the present study investigates the intention to adopt digital repositories among staff and students within the Malaysian Technical University Network (MTUN) on the basis of these factors. Guided by the UTAUT model, this study extends the model by integrating a green attitude into the framework to reflect the environmentally conscious viewpoint to explore how sustainability-oriented attitudes may influence technology adoption, supporting the shift toward more sustainable practices in higher education. As such, the following questions were formed to conduct this study. RQ1: Are there any effects of technological factors (performance expectancy, effort expectancy, facilitating conditions) on the intention to use digital repositories at the Malaysian Technical University Network (MTUN)? RQ2: Are there any effects of psychosocial factors (social influence, green attitude) on the intention to use digital repositories at the Malaysian Technical University Network (MTUN)? This study offers an empirical understanding of the underlying behavioural forces influencing the adoption of digital repositories in higher education, specifically the MTUN. This finding supports the theoretical advancement of the UTAUT model by incorporating an environmental dimension, i.e., a green attitude. Additionally, this study provides a practical direction for policymakers and institutional leaders in advancing and implementing successful digital strategies within the higher education landscape. The subsequent section provides a concise outline of the composition and development of the higher education system in Malaysia and the Malaysian Technical University Network. It is followed by a broad discussion of the literature on digital repositories and a detailed discussion of the theoretical framework used in this study, i.e., an extended UTAUT model. The methodology section details the measurement of items and outlines the development of the empirical model. It subsequently presents the data analysis and findings, contextualised through comparisons with findings from prior research. Finally, the study highlights key findings, limitations of research, and recommendations for future studies. 1.1. Higher education systems in Malaysia Malaysian higher education encompasses all postsecondary learning, training, and research provided by tertiary institutions such as universities and colleges (Kavithanjali, 2024). Historically, the system evolved through periods of British rule, which influenced its development (Zain et al., 2017). Today, Malaysian higher education offers programmes that enhance career prospects and professional growth across sectors (Malaysian Qualification Framework, 2017) that shape national progress, economic development, and a skilled workforce (OECD, 2018). The Ministry of Higher Education administers a diverse network of public and private institutions, such as universities, polytechnics, and community colleges, to ensure the success of the entire educational landscape (Ministry of Higher Education, Malaysia, 2022). Malaysia’s tertiary education system comprises 20 public institutions under university status, grouped into research, focused, and comprehensive institutions (Sheriff, 2017). It also encompasses 36 polytechnics, 105 community colleges, and 388 private colleges, collectively addressing academic and vocational needs (Ministry of Higher Education, Malaysia 2024). In line with the 12th Malaysian Plan (2022–2025), the government has increased funding for higher education to RM 16.3 billion, including RM 6.8 billion for Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET)-related programmes, indicating its importance for economic growth (Arumugam, 2021; Fadzil et al., 2022; MOF, 2023). TVET is central to Malaysia’s strategy for preparing a future-ready workforce, especially in the context of IR 4.0. It is supported through policies such as Shift No. 4 of the Malaysian Education Blueprint: Higher Education (MEB: HE 2015--2025), i.e., “Quality Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) Graduates”, which aligns with Sustainable Development https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Jaafar et al. Malaysian technical universities network (MTUN) The MTUN is crucial in strengthening TVET education because it supplies highly skilled professionals (Khan, 2018). Established in March 2006 and rebranded in February 2007, MTUN comprises of four universities: Universiti Teknologi Tun Hussein Onn Malaysia (UTHM), Universiti Teknikal Malaysia Melaka (UTeM), Universiti Malaysia Pahang Al-Sultan Abdullah (UMPSA), and Universiti Malaysia Perlis (UniMAP) (UTHM, 2025). These institutions offer undergraduate and postgraduate engineering, science, and technology programmes with a strong emphasis on applied research and high-impact innovation (Ministry of Higher Education Malaysia, 2015; Malaysia Board of Technologists, 2017). The MTUN is instrumental in preparing students for the workforce aligned with the Fourth Industrial Revolution (IR 4.0), as they serve as major contributors to the future job market (Sirat & Da Wan, 2018; Halili et al., 2021; Jam & Puteh, 2022). In today’s evolving economy, students must acquire a combination of technical, digital, and soft skills to remain competitive in the labour market (Motyl et al., 2017; World Economic Forum, 2017; Ismail & Hassan, 2019). The MTUN also drives innovation, technology transfer, and entrepreneurship, facilitating the relevance of Malaysia in the digital era (Hussin, 2018; Yusof, 2021). In partnership with industry and government bodies such as the National TVET Council (MTVET), the MTUN aligns academic programmes with industry needs to improve graduate employability (Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, 2023). Given its strategic importance, this study focuses on the MTUN to examine the factors influencing internal stakeholders' (staff and students) intention to use digital repositories. 2. Literature Review 2.1. Digital repositories A repository system is a digital service platform designed to ingest, store, manage, retrieve, display, and reuse digital content (Aboraya et al., 2021). An open archival information system concept offers a standardised foundation for building repositories. Such an organisation can establish this platform to manage digital documents, for instance, journal articles, theses, dissertations, datasets, audit documentation, teaching and learning materials, and conference papers (Hider et al., 2017; Pinfield, 2009). It emerged in the early 2000s, playing a critical role in knowledge and information management (Aboraya, 2022; Iris & Krystyna 2016). In addition, digital repository platforms help educational institutions manage, organise and preserve intellectual output while meeting teaching, research, and administrative needs (Aboraya, 2022; Anistyasari et al., 2018). Thus, it improves access to educational materials and supports learning objectives and outcomes, especially in online and distance learning (ODL) settings (Maldonado et al., 2016; Aboraya, 2022). This platform's functions can be integrated into wider digital strategies that store beyond academic content. The term "digital repositories" comprises institutional repositories, digital archives, and digital libraries; however, each item has slightly different functions. This research focuses on institutional repositories (IRs), digital archives managed by universities to preserve and provide access to intellectual output, teaching and administrative documents (Anenene et al., 2017; Saini, 2018). IRs often use open-source software such as E-Prints, DSpace, or Fedora, which help enhance the visibility of https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Jaafar et al. (2026) 4 academic work and promote open access through a centralised platform. In line with the recent demand for online education, digital repositories are important tools for supporting online activities that benefit e-learners (Aboraya, 2022; Ardura et al., 2025). 2.2. Past studies of technology adoption in higher education institutions Numerous papers have explored users' acceptance and adoption of various technologies in the higher education landscape. Observations from the literature revealed that the most frequently examined factors for technology adoption include perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness (Sambe & Raphael, 2015; Khan & Qutab, 2016; Anenene et al., 2017; Anistyasari et al., 2018; Xu & Du, 2018; Abdul Rahman & Mohezar, 2020), attitudes toward use (Khan & Qutab, 2016; Ammarukleart, 2017; Anenene et al., 2017; Dezdar, 2017; Akparobore & Omosekejimi, 2020), performance expectancy (Ammarukleart, 2017; Moorthy et al., 2019; Shivdas, et al., 2020; Wang, 2025), effort expectancy (Ammarukleart, 2017; Moorthy et al., 2019; Shivdas et al., 2020; Wang, 2025), social influence (Ammarukleart, 2017; Moorthy et al., 2019; Shivdas et al., 2020; Wang, 2025), and facilitating conditions (Ammarukleart, 2017). Findings from these studies have consistently revealed that performance expectancy (Ammarukleart, 2017; Shivdas et al., 2020; Wang, 2025), perceived usefulness and ease of use (Anenene et al., 2017; Anistyasari et al., 2018; Xu and Du, 2018, 2019), social influence (Ammarukleart, 2017; Wang, 2025) and facilitating conditions (Shivdas et al., 2020;) are significant determinants of technology adoption. Guided by this foundation, this study investigates the intention to adopt digital repositories among staff and students of the MTUN, which is divided into technological factors (i.e., performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and facilitating conditions) from the UTAUT model and psychosocial factors (social influence and green attitudes) from the UTAUT and TPB models. This integration offers a broad interpretation of the behavioural aspects of digital repository adoption in higher education, with a focus on the MTUN. 2.2.1. Performance expectancy Performance expectancy reflects an individual’s perception of how effectively technology can contribute to better performance (Venkatesh et al., 2016). This study reflects how staff and students at the MTUN perceive digital repositories as tools that could enhance academic productivity and working efficiency. Prevalently, users are more inclined to adopt such technology when they foresee its potential benefits, such as improving outcomes (Weeger et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2021; Gupta et al., 2019; Sharma et al., 2019; Almaiah et al., 2020; Dayour et al., 2020). Prior research has consistently revealed that performance expectancy is a key determining factor of technology acceptance and adoption, especially in educational settings (AlAwadhi & Morris, 2008; Cheok & Wong, 2015; Agag & Gomaa, 2016; Yang et al., 2019; Qiao et al., 2021; Raza et al., 2021; Wang, 2025). It also positively affects the use of digital academic resources by supporting research and access to information (Izuagbe, 2021; Nwone & Mutula, 2019). When users believe that technology will support them in achieving their goals, they will probably accept and use it. Grounded in the above arguments, the following hypotheses are formed: H1a: Performance expectancy affects the intention to use digital repositories among staff at the MTUN. H1b: Performance expectancy affects the intention to use digital repositories among students at the MTUN. 2.2.2. Effort expectancy Users' expectation of the level of ease in using a particular technology or system is known as effort expectancy (Venkatesh et al., 2016). Users are likely to adopt any technology if it has user-friendly features and requires minimal effort to used. This concept is the same as perceived ease of use and is frequently used interchangeably in technology acceptance research (Venkatesh et al., 2012). Several studies have revealed that effort expectancy extensively affects the behavioural intention to use diverse technologies, including mobile commerce, mobile learning, and mobile internet (Martins et al., 2014; Chaouali et al., 2016; Chao, 2019; Wong et al., 2019; Dagnoush & Khalifa, 2021). Additionally, the technology’s user-friendliness features have been recognised as crucial for long-term adoption (Gücin & Berk, 2015; Utomo et al., 2021). Thus, we hypothesise the following: H2a: Effort expectancy affects the intention to use digital repositories among staff at the MTUN. H2b: Effort expectancy affects the intention to use digital repositories among students at the MTUN. 2.2.3. Social influence Past studies revealed the importance of social influence in shaping users’ behavior, which is widely recognised as a key factor in technology adoption research. With the evolution of digital and social media technologies, social influence has played an important role in determining technology acceptance (Junglas et al., 2013; Tsai and Bagozzi, 2014; Graf-Vlachy et al., 2018). Social influence comprises i) normative influences, i.e., pressure to conform to others’ expectations, and ii) informational influence, i.e., stemming from advice or information received from others (Graf-Vlachy et al., 2018). Empirical evidence https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Jaafar et al. (2026) 5 indicates that social influence positively affects the adoption of various digital tools, including e-government platforms (Mensah, 2019), mobile and e-learning technologies (Alasmari & Zhang, 2019; Jacob & Pattusamy, 2020; Wang, 2025), and mobile nursing applications (Pan & Gao, 2021). On the basis of these conclusions, the following hypotheses are formulated: H3a: Social influence affects the intention to use digital repositories among staff at the MTUN. H3b: Social influence affects the intention to use digital repositories among students at the MTUN. 2.2.4. Facilitating conditions Facilitating conditions are users’ views of whether essential infrastructure, resources and technical support exist to encourage technology usage (Venkatesh et al., 2016). In addition, it includes compatibility with existing systems and ease of use. Different technologies require different levels of infrastructure; for example, health-related applications require reliable internet, proper devices, and digitally literate users (Utomo et al., 2021). Previous research has revealed that strong facilitating conditions positively influence the intention to adopt various technologies, such as e-government services (Mensah, 2019), mobile nursing apps (Pan & Gao, 2021) and mobile learning platforms (Izkair & Lakulu, 2021). Guided by these findings, the current study suggests that adequate facilitating conditions support the usage of digital repositories in higher education institutions. Thus, we hypothesise as follows: H4a: Facilitating conditions affect the intention to use digital repositories among staff at the MTUN. H4b: Facilitating conditions affect the intention to use digital repositories among students at the MTUN. 2.2.5. Green attitudes Green attitude is a person’s values, beliefs, and reactions toward environmental sustainability and conservation that motivate them to engage in eco-friendly behaviours when choosing products, services or technologies (Coskun, 2017). Several studies have revealed that attitudes significantly affect behavioural intentions across various contexts, including the use of social media for learning purposes (Yuan et al., 2021), online shopping for fashion products (Yusuf & Zulfitri, 2021), and the adoption of mobile health technologies (Hussein et al., 2017). Additionally, past research related to the environment has shown that those with strong green attitudes are more likely to favour and engage with eco-friendly technologies, whereas those with negative attitudes exhibit less passion (Amallia et al., 2021; Adinda Maharani et al., 2023). Hence, this study suggests that a positive green attitude influences the intention to use digital repositories among MTUN citizens, which supports environmental sustainability through paperless systems. Thus, the following hypotheses were developed: H5a: Green attitudes affect the intention to use digital repositories among the staff of the MTUN. H5b: Green attitudes affect the intention to use digital repositories among students of the MTUN. 2.3. Extended unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) The UTAUT model proposes four primary constructs (performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions) that could influence users’ behavioural intentions and actual technology use. These relationships are moderated by demographic factors such as gender, age, experience, and the voluntary nature of use (Venkatesh et al., 2003). It integrates eight established theories, such as the theory of reasoned action (TRA), the technology acceptance model (TAM), the motivational model, the theory of planned behaviour (TPB), a combined TAM/TPB model, the model of PC utilisation, innovation diffusion theory (IDT), and social cognitive theory (SCT). These models are broadly applied in numerous disciplines, such as information systems, marketing, social psychology, and management, to explore the determinants of the intention to adopt technology and its diffusion (Venkatesh et al., 2003; Williams et al., 2015). Past researchers such as Alwahaishi & Snášel (2013) and Venkatesh et al. (2016) highlight that performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and social influence are key determinants of technology adoption, whereas behavioural intention and facilitating conditions affect actual use. Meanwhile, moderating variables, i.e., gender, age, experience, and voluntariness, are hypothesised to strengthen these relationships to ensure that the model reflects diverse user behaviours. Collectively, these elements form a detailed framework for understanding and predicting technology adoption. To enhance the UTAUT framework, this study integrates the attitude construct from the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) (Ajzen, 1991). Attitude refers to an individual's overall assessment of performing a behaviour, which significantly influences their behavioural intention (Glanz et al., 2008). Since this study investigates the intention to adopt digital repositories, which are considered green infrastructures, a green attitude is proposed as an additional construct. By incorporating a green attitude with the four UTAUT constructs, this study suggests more robust insights into the behavioural dynamics affecting the intention to adopt digital repositories in higher education settings, as illustrated in Figure 2 below. Purposive sampling was used, which focuses on technical universities under the MTUN. We employed a stratified random sampling technique to ensure representative sampling, covering four MTUN institutions, i.e., UTeM, UTHM, UMPSA, and UniMAP. Staff were selected on the basis of staff directories available on the official websites of the respective universities, and the data were obtained via physical collection and an online Google form. Meanwhile, student participants were selected randomly across academic levels, with data collected via social media platforms such as Facebook, WhatsApp, and Instagram to increase accessibility and participation. The target sample size was guided by Krejcie and Morgan’s (1970) table, which recommended a minimum of 384 responses. However, 199 valid responses were collected. Despite being below the initial target, the sample size surpassed the minimum threshold for PLS-SEM analysis (160 responses) (Kock & Hadaya, 2018) and fulfilled the requirements for multigroup analysis (Kline, 2016; D’Souza et al., 2021). Furthermore, it aligns with established standards in behavioural research (Roscoe, 1975; Sekaran & Bougie, 2016; Hair et al., 2019). In addition, a G*Power assessment (effect size = 0.3) indicated that the minimum sample required for our dataset is only 111, confirming that this study's final sample of 199 provides adequate statistical power. The measurement of items adapted in this study were adapted from established measurement scales, comprising those established by Venkatesh et al. (2003). Each construct was operationalised into a collection of quantitative indicators and put into the survey instrument, allowing for a methodical evaluation of its effect on behavioural intention. Details of the measurement of the items are depicted in Table 1. The dataset was analysed via partial least squares-structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) via SmartPLS software. It is a broadly accepted technique in social science research for analysing complex models with small to medium-sized samples (Siyal et al., 2019; Shin & Lee, 2021; Albort-Morant et al., 2021). PLS-SEM is claimed to be suitable for exploratory research and supports formative and reflective measurement models (Hair et al., 2014; Henseler et al., 2016; Hair et al., 2019). Additionally, it allows the identification of underlying constructs and the modelling of complex relationships within datasets (Khmeleva et al., 2022). Measurement model analysis In research, assessing reliability and validity is critical to ensuring that the research instruments meet established methodological standards. Discussion This study analyses the effects of the UTAUT model and green attitudes on the intention to adopt digital repositories among MTUN staff and students. The findings revealed substantial differences between the two groups, offering important insights into enhancing digital adoption strategies in higher education settings. Notably, performance expectancy positively affects the intention to adopt digital repositories among MTUN staff but not students. This implies that staff who are more often involved in research, academic administration, and knowledge sharing are more encouraged by digital repositories' perceived usefulness and productivity benefits (Chao, 2019; Siripipatthanakul et al., 2022). In contrast, students may rely more on general academic tools and may not perceive digital repositories as necessary for their learning processes. Nevertheless, effort expectancy did not significantly affect the intention to adopt digital repositories in either group, supporting research by Mensah (2019) and Wang (2025) but opposed to studies that have shown a positive influence (Chaouali et al., 2016). This implies that when users are familiar with digital repositories and similar technologies, the ease of using the technology may not be a critical determinant of their behavioural intentions. Likewise, social influence is not a significant factor for either group. This condition may arise due to limited peer advocacy or consciousness surrounding the advantages of using digital repositories (Mensah, 2019; Alasmari & Zhang, 2019). The findings for facilitating conditions were similar to those for performance expectancy, where facilitating conditions significantly affected staff but not students. These circumstances highlight that institutional support, infrastructure readiness, and technical resources are more critical to staff, who often depend on such situations to perform their work efficiently (Pan & Gao, 2021; Izkair & Lakulu, 2021). On the other hand, students may be more technologically savvy, less reliant on institutional support systems, potentially hesitant to seek support when needed, or unaware of the institution's accessible support. Remarkably, a green attitude significantly influenced the intention to adopt digital repositories for both groups. This finding indicates that individuals with strong green values are likely to adopt paperless systems and engage in sustainable digital systems (Chawla & Joshi, 2019; Ali et al., 2023). Thus, promoting environmental awareness and sustainability practices may provide a convincing strategy to promote the acceptance of digital repositories in higher education institutions. This paper substantiates that distinctive motivational factors across user groups drive digital repository adoption. Performance expectancy and facilitating conditions are more significant for staff, whereas a green attitude is a key influence for both groups, specifically students. These outcomes imply the importance of tailoring promotional and implementation strategies according to user characteristics. Hence, higher education institutions should engage in strategic planning and evidence-based policymaking to ensure that capital investments in digital repositories as a form of green infrastructure are impactful and cost-effective. 6. Conclusions This study’s results provide valuable insights into the determinants of digital repository adoption among two groups of internal stakeholders (staff and students) in MTUN institutions. Despite its contributions, this study has several limitations. The exclusive use of a single approach, which is a quantitative approach with structured questionnaires, may limit the depth and richness of the findings, as it does not capture the multifaceted perceptions or contextual factors affecting users’ behaviour. Thus, future researchers could employ a mixed-method approach with a pragmatist philosophy to provide a comprehensive interpretation of user behaviour by combining statistical analysis with qualitative insights. In addition, this study focused solely on one institutional setting, which may restrict the generalisability of the results. Expanding the study's scope by considering a more diverse range of higher education institutions and incorporating user demographics as moderating variables will offer a more nuanced understanding of users’ behavioural patterns, which will enhance the pertinence of findings. In addition, future researchers could consider self-efficacy as a mediating variable to assess whether users' self-reliance in digital repositories independently impacts the strength of the relationships between the studied constructs and the intention to adopt them. By integrating self-efficacy into the framework, researchers may better encapsulate the psychological mechanisms underpinning technology adoption, thus strengthening the model’s explanatory power. Simultaneously, it could promote a more robust and comprehensive framework for understanding digital adoption in higher education settings. Finally, future studies may consider integrating other theoretical models, such as the technology-organisation- environment (TOE) framework (Tornatzky and Fleischer) or the information systems success (ISS) model (DeLone and McLean), https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Jaafar et al. (2026) 12 to enrich the conceptual understanding of technology adoption in the context of higher education. These guidelines could help shape more targeted and successful strategies for encouraging the use of digital repositories to promote national and global sustainability goals across institutions. JSON: Name: digital_repos_utaut_green_mtun Title: Multigroup PLS-SEM analysis of technological and psychosocial determinants of digital repository adoption in Malaysian technical universities Short Hypothesis: A stronger green attitude causes higher behavioural intention to use institutional digital repositories among staff and students in Malaysian technical universities. Related Work: Existing work on digital repository and digital-library adoption primarily applies technology acceptance frameworks (TAM, UTAUT, TPB) and finds that perceived usefulness/performance expectancy, perceived ease of use/effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions explain variance in behavioural intention. Some studies extend these models with environmental or attitude constructs for green IT contexts, while others add organisational or technical factors. Typical methodologies are cross-sectional surveys analysed with SEM (covariance- or variance-based) or regression; sample sizes are frequently small-to-moderate and analyses often aggregate heterogeneous user roles. Reported limitations include reliance on self-reported intention rather than observed usage, limited multigroup comparisons between role types (staff vs students), inconsistent inclusion of psychosocial sustainability constructs, insufficient tests for measurement invariance across groups, and sparse use of objective repository usage logs as validation. Current approaches therefore leave unresolved whether adding a green-attitude construct materially increases explanatory and predictive power across stakeholder groups and whether the effect generalises when validated against behavioural traces. Abstract: Problem: Adoption of institutional digital repositories in higher education remains low despite technical availability; the relative influence of technological constructs and sustainability-oriented psychosocial attitudes across staff and students is unclear. Approach: Use a stratified, multi-university survey of staff and students combined with institutional repository usage logs and apply multigroup Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to compare the standard UTAUT model against an extended UTAUT that includes green attitude and alternative mediators. Contribution: Quantify the causal effect of green attitude on intention to use and evaluate how adding green attitude changes explained variance, path significance, and out-of-sample predictive performance for staff versus students; validate intention results against observed repository activity. Expected outcome: A rigorously tested model that clarifies the role of green attitude relative to performance expectancy and facilitating conditions, demonstrates which predictors differ by role, and establishes whether self-reported intentions map to actual repository use. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Primary survey dataset: stratified sample across four MTUN universities targeting N>=400 (min 200 staff, 200 students). Survey items: validated scales for performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, green attitude, self-efficacy, behavioural intention; demographic controls (age, gender, role, experience). (2) Behavioral dataset: repository server logs (timestamped upload/download/self-archiving events) for same participants over a 6-month window, anonymized and joined via participant ID. Baselines: (A) UTAUT baseline (performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions -> intention). (B) UTAUT+green attitude. (C) UTAUT+green+self-efficacy mediator. (D) Behavioral outcome model: significant predictors -> actual repository activity (count and binary usage). Experimental procedure: 1) Measurement model assessment: Cronbach's alpha, composite reliability, AVE, item loadings, HTMT; ensure full measurement invariance across staff and students using MICOM procedure. 2) Structural model estimation: PLS-SEM with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Report path coefficients, t-values, p-values, f2 effect sizes, R2 for intention and for actual usage. 3) Multigroup analysis: permutation test of path differences between staff and student groups. 4) Predictive assessment: PLSpredict with 10-fold cross-validation; report RMSE and MAE for endogenous constructs. 5) Validation against behavioral logs: fit structural model using actual usage as endogenous variable (count modeled via negative binomial GLM or zero-inflated model) and compare sign and significance of predictors to intention model. Ablation studies: (i) remove green attitude from model and record ΔR2 and ΔPLSpredict metrics; (ii) remove facilitating conditions and record ΔR2; (iii) test model replacing intention with self-reported frequency to check measurement sensitivity. Evaluation metrics: measurement reliability/validity metrics (alpha, CR, AVE, HTMT), structural metrics (path coefficients, p-values, f2), model fit (SRMR), explanatory power (R2, adjusted R2), predictive power (PLSpredict RMSE/MAE), and goodness-of-fit for behavioral model (AIC/BIC, log-likelihood, pseudo-R2). Significance thresholds: p<0.05; report 95% bootstrap CIs. Controls: demographic covariates and experience as moderators in additional runs. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical and methodological failure modes: measurement non-invariance across staff and student groups preventing valid multigroup comparisons; high multicollinearity among predictors inflating VIFs and biasing path estimates; common-method bias from single-source self-report data. Data or evaluation biases: nonresponse bias in surveys, social desirability bias inflating green-attitude responses, sample not representative of broader higher-education populations beyond MTUN. Scalability and compute limitations: PLS-SEM bootstrap and PLSpredict with large bootstrap/sample splits may be computationally intensive if behavioral logs are large. Limits to generalization: cross-sectional design prevents causal claims about long-term adoption dynamics; results may not generalize to non-technical universities, other countries, or to different repository platforms. Behavioral-data linkage risks: incomplete or inconsistent linkage between survey IDs and repository logs; privacy or access restrictions may reduce behavioral sample size and create selection bias. Statistical power constraints: subgroup analyses require sufficient per-group N; small subgroup sizes will reduce ability to detect moderate effects.
